prize_parts.citation: for a visionary prose oeuvre, grounded in poetry, that builds memory, the body and dream into large-scale metaphysical architectures of the novel

statement.case_for: My preference for Cărtărescu stands after the exchange, but my claim is narrower than in round 1. On public knowledge, which I have not independently verified, the case rests on the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid. In these books a long-breathed, densely patterned voice treats inner experience as a cosmology. The work seems to me to belong to the European visionary and modernist tradition while remaining its own project. The architecture looks cumulative: the trilogy appears to build a structure in which recurring images carry the argument, and Solenoid reworks the same material in a different register. That is the best evidence I can point to that length is earned, though I cannot confirm it from the supplied descriptions. The poetry matters as formative ground, but I know it least well, so I now want the citation to rest on the prose and mention poetry only as the base. That changes the wording of my citation, not my ranking. The attribution is clean, with one writer and Romanian as the writing language. I still find the strongest combined case here on voice, formal ambition, imaginative depth and sustained quality. The fact that four members share this first choice is not part of my reasoning.
statement.case_against: The reservation I cannot remove is that the claim rests on translation and on the late novels. I cannot say how much of the density, rhythm and syntax belongs to the Romanian original. I also cannot say whether the long books sometimes let scale stand in for structure, as Olsson fears. My coverage of the poetry and early fiction is thin. If readers of Romanian reported that the late volumes repeat a method or lose tension, I would move toward Carson or Adonis. Carson's formal invention is more directly legible to us, as Sward argues. Adonis's remaking of a poetic language is a more clearly documented kind of linguistic achievement. These are real competitors, and I do not think the evidence supplied shows that either is weaker on the common criteria. The difference is mostly in what the committee can test.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis first for a decades-long remaking of Arabic poetic language and ranks Cărtărescu fourth because he doubts that the very long late volumes are evenly sustained. He also argues that the density of Cărtărescu's prose is as exposed to translation loss as Arabic verse, and that the citation for Adonis should rest on the poetry and not on the essays.
responses.response: I accept your correction on translation. In round 1 I said prose built on imagery and scale is less exposed than verse built on prosody. I still think that is probably so, but I cannot support it, and it should not count in Cărtărescu's favour. I now treat translation uncertainty as roughly equal for him and for Adonis. That leaves the evenness question, which is the real test of my case. I have no better evidence than public knowledge that the Blinding trilogy has a structure that holds. I would not ask you to take that on trust. I would support seeking Romanian readers' judgments on the later volumes, and I would want the same for Arabic readers on Adonis's later collections, put by the same questions. I agree that the citation for Adonis should stay on the poetry. I also agree that the age of an oeuvre does not decide anything for either of us.

responses.point: Sward ranks Carson first. She argues that grief, desire, the fragment and the afterlife of ancient texts recur across her essays, verse novel, elegy and later hybrids, so that the signal books are not isolated. She also argues that her English text is directly legible to the committee, and that her citation should rest on her own lyric and essayistic writing.
responses.response: Your answer on recurring concerns is stronger than I allowed in round 1. I had worried that Autobiography of Red and Nox were signal books with slighter volumes around them. A shared method across forms is a real argument for sustained quality, and I do not think the objection undermines the centre, as you say. I still think a prose architecture that is cumulative is easier to put in a single-writer citation than a hybrid practice where some of the invention is in the physical book. Even so, your point that Carson's text is directly legible to us is a real advantage for her. I do not claim it is outweighed. I keep Carson as my first alternative, and my reason for preferring Cărtărescu is a weighing of scale against formal reinvention. It is not a finding that her oeuvre is thinner.

responses.point: Mattson asks of Cărtărescu whether the long books earn their length through structure or whether scale sometimes substitutes for it. She wants any citation to say plainly that the claim concerns the prose project and not the full poetic corpus.
responses.response: I accept both points, and the second has changed my wording. The first is the test I would apply to my own case. The most I can say is that the trilogy reads as built up by recurrence and not by accumulation, and that is a judgment. My citation now names prose as the claim and poetry as a base. It does not claim the poetic corpus, because I cannot judge it. On whether density becomes mere pattern, I would not call this settled in the committee's favour, and I would give much weight to an expert reading before the vote.

responses.point: Palm argues that uneven quality in some volumes is a question about sustained quality that can be tested against the major works. She separates it from translation loss, which concerns whether we can see the achievement at all. She says the committee should state openly that the judgment is made through translation.
responses.response: I find the separation useful and I accept it. I would add one limit. If the trilogy and Solenoid carry the claim, an uneven minor volume matters less. But if the unevenness is inside those major books, the case is damaged. So the test has to be applied to the major works and not only to the minor ones. I agree that the committee should say openly that its judgment is made through translations. I would put that in the record next to the citation, for every candidate and not only for Cărtărescu.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first but names Adonis as her first alternative. She warns that she cannot judge Romanian density or the evenness of the long books, and that Adonis's Arabic prosody is a case she cannot test either.
responses.response: I agree with you on scope and on the shared limit. The prose should carry the citation, and neither of us can weigh Romanian density or Arabic prosody in the original. The chair asks whether the evidence for any leading candidate is too thin for P000. I do not think so. The case for each of the three is serious. But I hold my view conditionally, and I would rather the committee say so than treat it as closed.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's density, rhythm and syntax survives in translation. I cannot verify translation quality, and I now treat this exposure as comparable to Adonis's, not smaller.
Whether the long late novels, including the major books that carry the case, are evenly sustained or sometimes let scale replace structure. This cannot be settled from the supplied evidence.
My coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry and early fiction is partial, so the whole-oeuvre judgment rests mainly on the late prose.
Whether Adonis's later poetry matches his major collections, and whether Arabic prosody can be judged by readers working through translation.
How Carson's book-object, performance, scholarly and translation work should count in a citation limited to her own writing.
I have not independently verified any source. I rely on public knowledge and the shortlist descriptions, and I do not know what expert regional readings would show.
Carlberg's actual voting status is undocumented, so the simulated six-member vote and the four-vote majority are modeling assumptions.
statement.conflict_note: Updated. The profile records no personal connection to any shortlisted writer. I was elected alongside Ingrid Carlberg, who also prefers B042. That is a collegial tie and not a conflict, and her agreement is not part of my reasoning. My own work on Central Europe, Prague and Vienna, and the Nazi period touches the Magris entry (B004) thematically, but B004 is not a leading position and I do not rank it near my first choices. My practice as a novelist and critic is context only and is not evidence that I favour any candidate. I do not claim a conflict that requires recusal.
